sentences.text: Vouivria was a plant-eating sauropod dinosaur from the Brachiosauridae family that roamed what is now France during the Late Jurassic period.
The holotype, which serves as the primary specimen for the species, is an incomplete skeleton missing the head but containing many other bones.
This massive creature likely grew to a total length of fifteen meters and a mass of fifteen tonnes.
Measurements of the thighbone indicate it reached a length of 146 centimeters.
A distinctive ridge on the third metacarpal bone splits into a bulge near the upper quarter when the bone is held upright.
The fourth metacarpal features a flange running along the top third of its inner rear corner.
Two transverse ridges are located between the lower condyles of the femur at the junction with the rear shaft.
Well-formed laminae on the front and rear undersides of the transverse process help distinguish the front tail vertebrae from those of close relatives.
The humerus displays a deltopectoral crest that doubles in transverse width as it extends downward.
The genus name honors a French legend of a winged dragon or wyvern called la vouivre.
This name is a Latinization of the French word vouivre, which traces back to the Latin vipera, meaning viper.
If current research holds true, this animal might represent the oldest known brachiosaurid and the earliest member of the Titanosauriformes.
Laborers found large fossil bones at a chalkstone quarry near Damparis, France, in April 1934.
The excavation work started in May 1934 and finished on June 22, 1934.
Scientists Philip D. Mannion, Ronan Allain, and Olivier Moine formally named the genus Vouivria and its type species V. damparisensis in 2017.
These same researchers officially described the species Vouivria damparisensis in that year.
The specific name damparisensis indicates the animal's origin in the town of Damparis.
The bones were collected from a surface area covering approximately thirty square meters.
Evidence indicates the animal died close to a coastal lagoon, was scavenged by theropods, and was later buried by fresh chalk.

Researchers concluded in 2017 that the carcass died in place near a coastal lagoon, its weight created a slump in the soft chalk, it remained exposed for years while partially eaten by theropods, and was finally shielded by a new layer of hardened chalk.
Seven theropod teeth found among the remains were identified as belonging to Megalosaurus insignis.
Phylogenetic analysis places Vouivria as a basal member of the Brachiosauridae, situated between Europasaurus and Brachiosaurus altithorax.
Albert-Félix de Lapparent originally thought the specimen belonged to the Brachiosauridae family.
A 2017 phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Vouivria is a basal member of Brachiosauridae, positioned above Europasaurus and below Brachiosaurus altithorax on the evolutionary tree.
Vouivria lived approximately 163.5 to 157.3 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic.
The holotype was found in the Calcaires de Clerval formation, likely within the Tidalites member of Mouchard, dating to the middle to late Oxfordian stage.
The animal likely lived between 163.5 and 157.3 million years ago.
